final.title: When demo theatre quietly eats founder time
final.body:
If you run a 1–10 person business, demo theatre has a simple hidden cost: you spend time proving that something could work while the real workflow keeps waiting. That can happen when you keep polishing a demo, revisiting a POC, or trying one more tool instead of fixing the repetitive work already on your desk.

The real cost is not the demo itself. It is the time not spent on one recurring workflow with a measurable output. In a small business, that can look like repeated questions, manual data work, follow-ups, or invoice handling. Those are representative pains from the owner-operator scenario, not a market statistic or observed result. If the work is not repeating, AI is probably not the right place to start. No shame in that; the machine can wait.

Bareni’s diagnostic is deliberately bounded. We look for one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. Pilot timings and scope are intended, not guarantees. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle, though customers who want strategy only can choose a separate AI Strategy & Roadmap.

We also keep scope discipline: no high-sensitivity medical, legal, or financial work; no bulk cold-email automation; no scan-heavy OCR-dependent jobs; and no requests that depend on unsupported compliance or security claims. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A useful next step is to ask yourself: do I have one repeating workflow that takes roughly 5–10 hours a week, with output I can measure and approval that stays human? If not, demo theatre is probably the wrong place to spend the next hour.
